claim: Hydrostatic pressure increases linearly with depth in the ocean.
source: Hydrostatic pressure increases linearly with depth in the ocean and planktonic organisms can use it as a depth cue, which is independent of light or the time of the day (Blaxter, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Blaxter, 1978, indicating reliance on prior published work.

claim: Planktonic organisms can use hydrostatic pressure as a depth cue independent of light or time of day.
source: Hydrostatic pressure increases linearly with depth in the ocean and planktonic organisms can use it as a depth cue, which is independent of light or the time of the day (Blaxter, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Blaxter, 1978.

claim: Many marine invertebrate animals have long been known to sense and respond to changes in pressure.
source: Many marine invertebrate animals have long been known to sense and respond to changes in pressure (Knight-Jones and Qasim, 1955; Rice, 1964).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Knight-Jones and Qasim, 1955 and Rice, 1964.

claim: The response to pressure generally consists of an increase in locomotion (barokinesis) upon an increase in pressure.
source: The response generally consists of an increase in locomotion (barokinesis) upon an increase in pressure.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation in the text, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Barokinetic responses could help planktonic animals retain their depth either in combination with, or independent of light cues.
source: Such responses could help planktonic animals retain their depth either in combination with, or independent of light cues (Forward et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Forward et al., 1989.

claim: Changes in hydrostatic pressure may additionally entrain tidal rhythms in marine animals.
source: Changes in hydrostatic pressure may additionally entrain tidal rhythms in marine animals (Akiyama, 2004; Morgan, 1965; Naylor and Williams, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akiyama, 2004; Morgan, 1965; Naylor and Williams, 1984.

claim: Early studies on the barokinetic response in zooplankton have not revealed if the animals respond to relative or absolute changes in pressure.
source: Early studies on the barokinetic response in zooplankton have not revealed if the animals respond to relative or absolute changes in pressure.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of prior research, drawing on knowledge of the literature.

claim: The kinematics and neuronal mechanisms of pressure responses have not been characterized in detail for any planktonic animal.
source: The kinematics and neuronal mechanisms of pressure responses have also not been characterized in detail for any planktonic animal.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of prior research, drawing on knowledge of the literature.

claim: The most familiar structures for sensing changes in hydrostatic pressure are gas-filled compressible vesicles such as the swim bladder in fish.
source: The most familiar structures for sensing changes in hydrostatic pressure are gas-filled compressible vesicles such as the swim bladder in fish (Qutob, 1963).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Qutob, 1963.

claim: Barokinetic responses are seen across many animals without any identifiable gas-filled vesicles.
source: However, barokinetic responses are seen across many animals without any identifiable gas-filled vesicles.
evidence: This is stated as an observation drawing on established knowledge.

claim: In the statocyst of the adult crab Carcinus maenas, millimeter-sized thread-hairs may act as a syringe plunger to sense pressure.
source: In the statocyst of the adult crab Carcinus maenas, millimeter-sized thread-hairs may act as a syringe plunger to sense pressure (Fraser and Macdonald, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fraser and Macdonald, 1994.

claim: In dogfish, which lack a swim bladder, hair cells in the vestibular organ have been proposed to act as pressure detectors.
source: In dogfish, which lack a swim bladder, hair cells in the vestibular organ have been proposed to act as pressure detectors (Fraser and Shelmerdine, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fraser and Shelmerdine, 2002.

claim: It is unknown which, if any, of the two vastly different pressure sensing mechanisms is used by the much smaller planktonic animals.
source: It is unknown which, if any, of these two vastly different pressure sensing mechanisms—one based on volume changes in a gas-filled vesicle and the other on deformation of sensory cilia—is used by the much smaller planktonic animals.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The planktonic ciliated larvae of the marine annelid Platynereis dumerilii use ciliary beating to swim up and down in the water column.
source: This larva uses ciliary beating to swim up and down in the water column to eventually settle on sea grass beds near coastal regions (Gambi et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gambi et al., 1992.

claim: Platynereis larvae eventually settle on sea grass beds near coastal regions.
source: This larva uses ciliary beating to swim up and down in the water column to eventually settle on sea grass beds near coastal regions (Gambi et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gambi et al., 1992.

claim: The sensory and neuronal bases of light-guided behaviours in Platynereis larvae have been dissected.
source: The sensory and neuronal bases of light-guided (Gühmann et al., 2015; Randel et al., 2014; Verasztó et al., 2018) and mechanically driven behaviours (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018) in Platynereis larvae have been dissected due to the experimental tractability of this system.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gühmann et al., 2015; Randel et al., 2014; Verasztó et al., 2018.

claim: The sensory and neuronal bases of mechanically driven behaviours in Platynereis larvae have been dissected.
source: The sensory and neuronal bases of light-guided (Gühmann et al., 2015; Randel et al., 2014; Verasztó et al., 2018) and mechanically driven behaviours (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018) in Platynereis larvae have been dissected due to the experimental tractability of this system.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018.

claim: The entire cellular and synaptic wiring map of the 3-day-old Platynereis larva has been reconstructed.
source: Its small size has allowed the entire reconstruction of the cellular and synaptic wiring map of the 3-day-old larva (Jasek et al., 2022; Verasztó et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jasek et al., 2022; Verasztó et al., 2024.

claim: Both 2- and 3-day-old Platynereis larvae respond to pressure increase by swimming upwards faster and in straighter trajectories.
source: Both 2- and 3-day-old larvae respond to pressure increase by swimming upwards faster and in straighter trajectories, as quantified by changes in average vertical displacement, swimming speed, the ratio of upward to downward trajectories (Figure 1B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D; Video 1), and a straightness index (the net over total distance) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D, and Video 1.

claim: In both 2- and 3-day-old larvae, the responses to pressure were graded: higher pressure levels led to higher maximal vertical displacement.
source: In both 2- and 3-day-old larvae, the responses were graded: higher pressure levels led to higher maximal vertical displacement (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, E.

claim: Three-day-old larvae had a slightly lower sensitivity threshold (10–20 mbar) than 2-day-old larvae (20–30 mbar).
source: Three-day-old larvae had a slightly lower sensitivity threshold (10–20 mbar) than 2-day-old larvae (20–30 mbar) and their response plateaued at lower pressure levels than that of 2-day-old larvae (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B–E.

claim: The response of 3-day-old larvae plateaued at lower pressure levels than that of 2-day-old larvae.
source: Three-day-old larvae had a slightly lower sensitivity threshold (10–20 mbar) than 2-day-old larvae (20–30 mbar) and their response plateaued at lower pressure levels than that of 2-day-old larvae (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B–E.

claim: One-day-old larvae did not show a detectable response to even the largest pressure levels tested.
source: One-day-old larvae did not show a detectable response to even the largest pressure levels tested (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: The straightness of trajectories increased with increasing pressure changes.
source: The straightness of trajectories also increased with increasing pressure changes.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Narrower helical swimming paths under pressure were visible in close-up videos.
source: This was due to narrower helical swimming paths under pressure, visible in close-up videos (Video 2 and Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by video data (Video 2 and Video 3).

claim: Three-day-old larvae showed a diving response upon the release of pressure.
source: Three-day-old larvae also showed a diving response upon the release of pressure (Figure 1B, C, F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, C, F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Two-day-old larvae stopped moving upwards when the stimulus ended, but did not show an active diving response to pressure OFF.
source: Two-day-old larvae stopped moving upwards when the stimulus ended, but did not show an active diving response to pressure OFF.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Platynereis larvae showed the same dependence of vertical displacement on the magnitude of pressure change when a static column of water of different heights was used to change pressure levels.
source: To exclude the possibility that either the changes in the partial pressure of gases due to the use of compressed air, or the mechanical wave associated to the inflow of air caused the upward swimming behaviour, we also used a static column of water of different heights to change pressure levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C). We observed the same dependence of vertical displacement on the magnitude of pressure change in this setup (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, D, E.

claim: Larvae compensate for the increase in pressure by a corresponding increase in upward swimming when rates of pressure increase are sufficiently high.
source: These results suggest that larvae compensate for the increase in pressure by a corresponding increase in upward swimming when rates of pressure increase are sufficiently high.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results on linear increases of pressure.

claim: The linear response to a gradual increase in pressure suggests that larvae detect changes in pressure, rather than absolute pressure levels.
source: The linear response to a gradual increase in pressure suggests that larvae detect changes in pressure, rather than absolute pressure levels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Larvae reacted with graded upward swimming even if they were pre-exposed to 100 or 500 mbar.
source: Upon step increase, larvae reacted with graded upward swimming even if they were pre-exposed to 100 or 500 mbar (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The sensitivity decreased when larvae were acclimated to 500 mbar.
source: The sensitivity decreased when larvae were acclimated to 500 mbar (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Larvae pre-exposed to 500 mbar showed a downward displacement followed by an upward displacement as soon as pressure was increased back to the corresponding basal level.
source: When pressure was released at the end of the increase trials, larvae pre-exposed to 500 mbar showed a downward displacement followed by an upward displacement as soon as pressure was increased back to the corresponding basal level (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3G.

claim: Platynereis larvae react to relative increases in pressure in a graded manner proportional to the magnitude of the increase.
source: Our experiments suggest that Platynereis larvae react to relative increases in pressure in a graded manner proportional to the magnitude of the increase.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The response of Platynereis larvae to pressure is adaptable and occurs at very different basal pressures (0 or 500 mbar—corresponding to surface or 5 m of water depth).
source: The response is adaptable and occurs at very different basal pressures (0 or 500 mbar—corresponding to surface or 5 m of water depth).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The mean ciliary beat frequency (CBF) increased as soon as a step change in pressure was applied, with larger step changes showing more noticeable increases in beat frequency.
source: The mean ciliary beat frequency (CBF) increased as soon as a step change in pressure was applied, with larger step changes showing more noticeable increases in beat frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C, Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C and Video 4.

claim: The maximum ciliary beat frequency (max. CBF) during the stimulus period showed a statistically significant increase for all but the lowest pressure steps tested relative to the period before the onset of the stimulus.
source: The maximum ciliary beat frequency (max. CBF) during the stimulus period showed a statistically significant increase for all but the lowest pressure steps tested relative to the period before the onset of the stimulus (85 mb p = 0.046, 237.5 mb p = 2.08E−05, 556 mb p = 8.35E−07, 988 mb p = 7.8E−07; one-tailed paired t-test with Bonferroni correction testing for an increase in CBF; Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Rapid upward swimming under pressure is due to an increase in the beating frequency of prototroch cilia that is proportional to the change in pressure.
source: Overall, these data suggest that rapid upward swimming under pressure is due to an increase in the beating frequency of prototroch cilia that is proportional to the change in pressure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results on ciliary beat frequency.

claim: A group of four cells in the dorsomedial brain showed consistent increases in GCaMP6s fluorescence when pressure increased.
source: By imaging the entire larva before and during the pressure stimulus, we found a group of four cells in the dorsomedial brain that showed consistent increases in GCaMP6s fluorescence when pressure increased (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The four cells activated under pressure had prominent cilia, which become visible by the increase in GCaMP6s signal during pressure increase.
source: Time-lapse (TL) recordings of these cells revealed that they had prominent cilia, which become visible by the increase in GCaMP6s signal during pressure increase (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Video 1.

claim: The position, number, size, and morphology of the four cells activated under pressure closely matched to that of the previously described brain ciliary photoreceptor cells (cPRCs).
source: The position, number, size, and morphology of these cells closely matched to that of the previously described brain ciliary photoreceptor cells (cPRCs) (Arendt et al., 2004; Tsukamoto et al., 2017; Verasztó et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arendt et al., 2004; Tsukamoto et al., 2017; Verasztó et al., 2018.

claim: Immunostaining with an antibody raised against NIT-GC2 directly confirmed that the four cells activated under pressure were the cPRCs.
source: Immunostaining of the same larvae that were used for Ca2+ imaging with an antibody raised against NIT-GC2, a marker of cPRC cilia(Jokura et al., 2023), followed by image registration directly confirmed that the four cells activated under pressure were the cPRCs (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and a citation to Jokura et al., 2023.

claim: All four cPRCs responded to the pressure levels tested.
source: All four cPRCs responded to the pressure levels tested (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: The increase in GCaMP6s signal in cPRCs was observed in both the cell body and in the cilia.
source: The increase in GCaMP6s signal was observed in both the cell body and in the cilia of the cPRCs (Figure 2C, Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Video 5.

claim: The cPRC response to pressure was graded and increased proportionally to the pressure change.
source: This response—like that observed at the behavioural level—was graded and increased proportionally to the pressure change (Figure 2E, F; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C, E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E, F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C, E.

claim: The difference in the cPRC response between pressure levels was statistically significant for some of the cPRCs.
source: The difference in the response between pressure levels was statistically significant for some of the cPRCs (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The calcium signal in cPRCs decreased rapidly after stimulus onset.
source: The calcium signal also decreased rapidly after stimulus onset.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: cPRCs may be able to directly encode the intensity of the stimulation in their activity, reflected in their internal Ca2+ levels, and adapt to pressure levels.
source: Therefore, cPRCs may be able to directly encode the intensity of the stimulation in their activity, reflected in their internal Ca2+ levels, and adapt to pressure levels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results on calcium dynamics.

claim: The unique sensory morphology and pressure-induced Ca2+ dynamics make the cPRCs candidate pressure receptors.
source: Their unique sensory morphology and pressure-induced Ca2+ dynamics make the cPRCs candidate pressure receptors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: An additional unpaired sensory cell on the dorsal side (SNd1_unp) was also activated in some of the trials.
source: An additional unpaired sensory cell on the dorsal side was also activated in some of the trials (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, green asterisk).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 750 mb, SNd1_unp responded by a transient but robust increase at stimulation onset, but ∆R/R dropped to basal values before the end of the stimulus, unlike the cPRC response.
source: At 750 mb, this cell responded by a transient but robust increase at stimulation onset, but ∆R/R dropped to basal values before the end of the stimulus, unlike the cPRC response (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: SNd1_unp may also contribute to the pressure response, although it is less sensitive than cPRCs and has very few synapses.
source: SNd1_unp (SNYFa+) may also contribute to the pressure response, although it is less sensitive than cPRCs and has very few synapses (Williams et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and supported by a citation to Williams et al., 2017.

claim: One-day-old larvae that lack differentiated cPRCs do not respond to pressure.
source: Another indirect observation that is consistent with cPRCs being the primary pressure receptors is that 1-day-old larvae that lack differentiated cPRCs (Fischer et al., 2010) do not respond to pressure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and a citation to Fischer et al., 2010.

claim: cPRCs express ciliary-opsin-1 (c-ops-1), which forms a UV-absorbing photopigment.
source: cPRCs express ciliary-opsin-1 (c-ops-1), which forms a UV-absorbing photopigment (Arendt et al., 2004; Tsukamoto et al., 2017; Verasztó et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arendt et al., 2004; Tsukamoto et al., 2017; Verasztó et al., 2018.

claim: Knocking out the c-ops-1 gene abolishes a UV-avoidance response in Platynereis larvae.
source: Knocking out the c-ops-1 gene abolishes a UV-avoidance response in Platynereis larvae (Verasztó et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Verasztó et al., 2018.

claim: The swimming speed of c-ops-1∆8/∆8 mutant larvae was not significantly different from WT larvae.
source: The swimming speed of c-ops-1∆8/∆8 mutant larvae was not significantly different from WT larvae (p = 0.118, unpaired Wilcoxon test for lower speed in mutants; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae responded in a graded manner to increases in pressure by upward swimming.
source: c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae responded in a graded manner to increases in pressure by upward swimming (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The response of c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae to pressure was weaker than the response of age-matched WT larvae.
source: However, their response was weaker than the response of age-matched WT larvae (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: An ANOVA comparison showed that a model considering the genotype better explained the data than a model without this variable, for either a simple or a polynomial linear regression model.
source: An ANOVA comparison showed that a model considering the genotype better explained the data than a model without this variable, for either a simple or a polynomial linear regression model (p-values = 9.98e−0⁷ and 9.92e−⁰⁶, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Ciliary beating prior to pressure increase was not significantly different between c-ops-1∆8/∆8 and WT larvae.
source: Ciliary beating prior to pressure increase was not significantly different between c-ops-1∆8/∆8 and WT larvae (p = 0.835, unpaired Wilcoxon test for lower CBF in mutants; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Upon pressure increases, CBF in c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae showed a significant increase to the three highest pressure levels tested.
source: Upon pressure increases, CBF in c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae showed a significant increase to the three highest pressure levels tested (237.5 mb p = 0.014, 556 mb p = 9.7E−05, 988 mb p = 6.35E−05; one-tailed paired t-test with Bonferroni correction testing for an increase in CBF; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae can still respond to changes in pressure in a graded manner, but the response is weaker than in WT larvae, both at the population and at the single-larva levels.
source: In summary, c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae can still respond to changes in pressure in a graded manner, but the response is weaker than in WT larvae, both at the population and at the single-larva levels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: c-opsin-1 is not directly required for the pressure response, but its absence leads to a weakened response to pressure.
source: This indicates that c-opsin-1 is not directly required for the pressure response, but its absence leads to a weakened response to pressure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The reduced response of c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae to pressure may stem from morphological defects of the cPRC sensory cilia in these mutants.
source: The reduced response of c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae to pressure may stem from morphological defects of the cPRC sensory cilia in these mutants.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the experimental results.

claim: The cPRC ciliary compartment in c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae was significantly smaller than in age-matched WT larvae.
source: Volumetric imaging in 2-day-old larvae stained with these antibodies revealed that the cPRC ciliary compartment in c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae was significantly smaller than in age-matched WT larvae (p = 0.044 and 0.018 for left and right ciliary compartments, one-tailed unpaired t-test with Bonferroni correction; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In some cases, cPRC ciliary compartments were drastically reduced, albeit never completely absent in all four cells.
source: In some cases, cPRC ciliary compartments were drastically reduced, albeit never completely absent in all four cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: A reduced ciliary compartment may underlie the weaker responses of c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae to pressure.
source: A reduced ciliary compartment may underlie the weaker responses of c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae to pressure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The two WT cPRCs reconstructed have 14 to 15 ramified cilia tightly wrapped on themselves.
source: The two WT cPRCs reconstructed have 14 to 15 ramified cilia tightly wrapped on themselves (Figure 3E, top row, Video 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Video 6.

claim: Branching in WT cPRC cilia occurs close to the basal body, soon after cilia protrude from the cell body.
source: Branching occurs close to the basal body, soon after cilia protrude from the cell body.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the electron microscopy data.

claim: Most branches in WT cPRC cilia inherit an individual microtubule doublet.
source: Most branches inherit an individual microtubule doublet.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the electron microscopy data.

claim: The 15 to 17 cilia of the two cPRCs reconstructed in a c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larva revealed a more sparsely packed structure.
source: The 15 to 17 cilia of the two cPRCs reconstructed in a c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larva revealed a more sparsely packed structure (Figure 3E, bottom row; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Video 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and Video 7.

claim: Mutant cPRC cilia are not significantly shorter than WT cPRC cilia.
source: Mutant cilia are not significantly shorter than WT cPRC cilia (p = 0.076, Wilcoxon test for longer WT cilia, Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Individual branches of mutant cPRC cilia often contained more than one microtubule doublet.
source: However, we noticed when comparing cross-sections of each genotype that individual branches of mutant cPRC cilia often contained more than one microtubule doublet (arrowheads in Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: cPRC cilia of c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae have alterations in branching morphology.
source: This suggests that cPRC cilia of c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae have alterations in branching morphology.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the electron microscopy data.

claim: The terminal branches of cilia in the c-ops-1∆8/∆8 mutant are significantly shorter.
source: We indeed found that the terminal branches of cilia in the mutant are significantly shorter (p = 6.29E−05 Wilcoxon test for shorter branches in the mutant, Figure 3G, right-most plot), while internal branches are longer than those in the WT (p = 1.26E−04; Wilcoxon test for longer branches in the mutant, Figure 3G, middle plot).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Internal branches of cilia in the c-ops-1∆8/∆8 mutant are longer than those in the WT.
source: We indeed found that the terminal branches of cilia in the mutant are significantly shorter (p = 6.29E−05 Wilcoxon test for shorter branches in the mutant, Figure 3G, right-most plot), while internal branches are longer than those in the WT (p = 1.26E−04; Wilcoxon test for longer branches in the mutant, Figure 3G, middle plot).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Basal branches in c-ops-1∆8/∆8 mutant cPRC cilia tended to be larger, but no statistically significance can be concluded.
source: Basal branches also tended to be larger, but no statistically significance can be concluded (p = 0.06, Wilcoxon test for longer branches in the mutant, Figure 3G, left-most plot).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Branching occurs more distally to the basal body in c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae.
source: This result supports the former observation that branching occurs more distally to the basal body in c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Longer internal branches in mutant cPRC cilia would explain the presence of ciliary profiles with more than one microtubule doublet.
source: Longer internal branches in mutant cPRC cilia would also explain the presence of ciliary profiles with more than one microtubule doublet (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The brain cPRCs act as graded and fast-adapting pressure receptors.
source: Overall, our physiological and genetic analyses suggest that the brain cPRCs act as graded and fast-adapting pressure receptors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: In c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae, the ciliary compartment is smaller and shows morphological defects, revealing a genetic requirement for c-opsin-1 in the establishment of the sensory compartment.
source: In c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae, the ciliary compartment is smaller and shows morphological defects, revealing a genetic requirement for c-opsin-1 in the establishment of the sensory compartment and supporting the idea that the cPRC ciliary compartment is the site of pressure transduction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The cPRC ciliary compartment is the site of pressure transduction.
source: In c-ops-1∆8/∆8 larvae, the ciliary compartment is smaller and shows morphological defects, revealing a genetic requirement for c-opsin-1 in the establishment of the sensory compartment and supporting the idea that the cPRC ciliary compartment is the site of pressure transduction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The complete synaptic wiring diagram of the cPRCs was previously reported from an electron microscopy volume of a 3-day-old larva.
source: The complete synaptic wiring diagram of the cPRCs was previously reported from an electron microscopy volume of a 3-day-old larva (Figure 4A, B; Verasztó et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Verasztó et al., 2018 and shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: The shortest neuronal path from cPRCs to the prototroch involves a feed-forward loop from the cPRCs to two types of postsynaptic interneurons: the INNOS and the INRGWa cells.
source: The shortest neuronal path from cPRCs to the prototroch involves a feed-forward loop from the cPRCs to two types of postsynaptic interneurons: the INNOS and the INRGWa cells, expressing respectively Nitric Oxide Synthase (NOS) or the neuropeptide RGWamide (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated based on the synaptic wiring diagram shown in Figure 4B.

claim: INRGWa cells synapse on a pair of head serotonergic ciliomotor neurons (Ser-h1).
source: INRGWa cells in turn synapse on a pair of head serotonergic ciliomotor neurons (Ser-h1).
evidence: This is stated based on the synaptic wiring diagram.

claim: Ser-h1 cells directly innervate the prototroch ciliary band and synapse on the MC head cholinergic ciliomotor neuron.
source: Ser-h1 cells directly innervate the prototroch ciliary band and synapse on the MC head cholinergic ciliomotor neuron (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated based on the synaptic wiring diagram shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ser-h1 cells are thought to promote ciliary beating by directly releasing serotonin onto the ciliary band cells and indirectly by inhibiting the cholinergic MC neuron that is required to arrest ciliary beating.
source: Ser-h1 cells are thought to promote ciliary beating by directly releasing serotonin onto the ciliary band cells and indirectly by inhibiting the cholinergic MC neuron that is required to arrest ciliary beating (Verasztó et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Verasztó et al., 2017.

claim: Larvae expressing TeTxLC in Ser-h1 showed an increase in CBF only at the highest pressure used (988 mb).
source: Larvae expressing TeTxLC in Ser-h1 showed an increase in CBF only at the highest pressure used (988 mb p = 0.004; one-tailed paired t-test with Bonferroni correction testing for an increase in CBF; Figure 4E, bottom row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Larvae injected with a control plasmid expressing only Palmi-tdTomato but not TeTxLC in Ser-h1 showed a significant increase in CBF at the three highest pressure levels applied.
source: Larvae injected with a control plasmid expressing only Palmi-tdTomato but not TeTxLC in Ser-h1 (Figure 4C) showed a significant increase in CBF at the three highest pressure levels applied (237.5 mb p = 0.023, 556 mb p = 0.009, 988 mb p = 0.004; one-tailed paired t-test with Bonferroni correction testing for an increase in CBF; Figure 4E, top row; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TeTxLC-mediated inhibition of Ser-h-1 leads to a noticeable dampening of the pressure response at the level of the ciliary band.
source: These results indicate that TeTxLC-mediated inhibition of Ser-h-1—albeit incomplete and in most cases limited to one of the two cells—leads to a noticeable dampening of the pressure response at the level of the ciliary band.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Synaptic release from serotonergic neurons is required to increase ciliary beating upon pressure increase.
source: This suggests that synaptic release from serotonergic neurons is required to increase ciliary beating upon pressure increase.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Ser-h1 neurons, and no other serotonergic cells, are specifically required for the pressure response.
source: Our data support the model that Ser-h1 neurons, and no other serotonergic cells, are specifically required for this response, because this cell type was labelled in all animals tested and these cells directly innervate the prototroch.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Increased pressure induced a rapid, graded, and adapting upward swimming response due to the faster beating of cilia in the head multiciliary band.
source: Increased pressure induced a rapid, graded, and adapting upward swimming response due to the faster beating of cilia in the head multiciliary band.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the findings.

claim: Brain ciliary photoreceptors showed a graded response to pressure changes.
source: By calcium imaging, we found that brain ciliary photoreceptors showed a graded response to pressure changes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the findings.

claim: The photoreceptors in animals mutant for ciliary opsin-1 had a smaller sensory compartment and mutant larvae showed diminished pressure responses.
source: The photoreceptors in animals mutant for ciliary opsin-1 had a smaller sensory compartment and mutant larvae showed diminished pressure responses.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the findings.

claim: The ciliary photoreceptors synaptically connect to the head multiciliary band via serotonergic motoneurons.
source: The ciliary photoreceptors synaptically connect to the head multiciliary band via serotonergic motoneurons.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the findings.

claim: Genetic inhibition of the serotonergic cells blocked pressure-dependent increases in ciliary beating.
source: Genetic inhibition of the serotonergic cells blocked pressure-dependent increases in ciliary beating.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the findings.

claim: Ciliary photoreceptors function as pressure sensors and activate ciliary beating through serotonergic signalling during barokinesis.
source: We conclude that ciliary photoreceptors function as pressure sensors and activate ciliary beating through serotonergic signalling during barokinesis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Increases in pressure, either due to the larva's own actions (sinking or diving) or to downwelling currents, lead to the activation of the sensory cPRCs.
source: Our findings suggest that increases in pressure, either due to the larva's own actions (sinking or diving) or to downwelling currents, lead to the activation of the sensory cPRCs (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The activation of cPRCs is proportional to the magnitude of pressure change and leads to the activation of the downstream circuit that converges onto the Ser-h1 neurons and ultimately leads to increased ciliary beating.
source: The activation is proportional to the magnitude of pressure change and leads to the activation of the downstream circuit that converges onto the Ser-h1 neurons and ultimately leads to increased ciliary beating.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings.

claim: The Ser-h1 cells could secrete serotonin (5-HT) onto the ciliary band, which from pharmacological assays is known to increase CBF.
source: The Ser-h1 cells could secrete serotonin (5-HT) onto the ciliary band, which from pharmacological assays is known to increase CBF (Verasztó et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Verasztó et al., 2017.

claim: Ser-h1 neurons may simultaneously inhibit the cholinergic ciliomotoneuron MC neuron, thereby preventing ciliary arrests while the larva tries to compensate for the increased pressure.
source: Ser-h1 neurons may simultaneously inhibit the cholinergic ciliomotoneuron MC neuron (Verasztó et al., 2017), thereby preventing ciliary arrests while the larva tries to compensate for the increased pressure.
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Verasztó et al., 2017.

claim: Upon a decrease in pressure, 3-day-old (but not 2-day-old) larvae show an off-response characterized by downward swimming.
source: Upon a decrease in pressure, 3-day-old (but not 2-day-old) larvae also show an off-response characterized by downward swimming.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings.

claim: The pressure off-response may depend on an inverted activation of the cPRC circuit, as happens during UV avoidance.
source: We have not analysed in detail the neuronal mechanisms of this response but it may depend on an inverted activation of the cPRC circuit, as happens during UV avoidance (Jokura et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to Jokura et al., 2023.

claim: Pressure 'on' and pressure 'off' induce behavioural responses with opposite sign such that larvae move to compensate for the pressure change.
source: Pressure 'on' and pressure 'off' thus induce behavioural responses with opposite sign such that larvae move to compensate for the pressure change.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The response is directional along the pressure gradient (even if larvae do not detect the gradient but temporal changes) and is referred to as barotaxis.
source: The response is directional along the pressure gradient (even if larvae do not detect the gradient but temporal changes) and we refer to it as barotaxis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The proposed depth-retention model complements a previously reported spectral depth-gauge mechanism in the Platynereis larva based on its ability to respond to UV and green light.
source: Our proposed depth-retention model complements a previously reported spectral depth-gauge mechanism in the Platynereis larva based on its ability to respond to UV and green light (Verasztó et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Verasztó et al., 2018.

claim: Pressure sensing in Platynereis may operate through negative feedback to retain a particular depth, while light as a more variable stimulus could drive intensity and wavelength-dependent changes in the vertical position of larvae.
source: As previously hypothesized for other planktonic larvae (Sulkin, 1984), pressure sensing in Platynereis may operate through negative feedback to retain a particular depth, while light as a more variable stimulus could drive intensity and wavelength-dependent changes in the vertical position of larvae.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to Sulkin, 1984.

claim: Ciliary photoreceptors, previously shown to be sensitive to UV and green light, are also activated by pressure increase.
source: Our unexpected finding that ciliary photoreceptors, previously shown to be sensitive to UV and green light (Verasztó et al., 2018), are also activated by pressure increase suggests that the integration of light and pressure could begin at the sensory level in a single-cell type.
evidence: This is stated as a finding and supported by a citation to Verasztó et al., 2018.

claim: The integration of light and pressure could begin at the sensory level in a single-cell type.
source: Our unexpected finding that ciliary photoreceptors, previously shown to be sensitive to UV and green light (Verasztó et al., 2018), are also activated by pressure increase suggests that the integration of light and pressure could begin at the sensory level in a single-cell type.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: UV light activates the cPRCs to induce downward swimming while pressure increases induce upward swimming.
source: UV light activates the cPRCs to induce downward swimming while pressure increases induce upward swimming.
evidence: This is stated as an observation drawing on established knowledge and the current findings.

claim: The calcium dynamics of cPRCs depends on the stimulus applied and may therefore underlie the mechanism by which the cells decode and transmit a sensory signal to the downstream circuit.
source: The calcium dynamics of cPRCs depends on the stimulus applied and may therefore underlie the mechanism by which the cells decode and transmit a sensory signal to the downstream circuit.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: UV induces a transient increase and subsequent drop in Ca2+ levels followed by a sharp NO-dependent increase that persists even after UV stimulation ends.
source: UV induces a transient increase and subsequent drop in Ca2+ levels followed by a sharp NO-dependent increase that persists even after UV stimulation ends (Jokura et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jokura et al., 2023.

claim: Pressure induces a transient increase in Ca2+ levels that terminates with the stimulus.
source: In contrast, pressure induces a transient increase in Ca2+ levels that terminates with the stimulus.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The different activation dynamics may lead to the release of different neurotransmitter and neuromodulator cocktails.
source: The different activation dynamics may lead to the release of different neurotransmitter and neuromodulator cocktails cPRCs are cholinergic, GABAergic, adrenergic, and peptidergic (Jokura et al., 2023; Randel et al., 2014; Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2017) and different activation patterns in the postsynaptic cells.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Jokura et al., 2023; Randel et al., 2014; Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2017.

claim: cPRCs are cholinergic, GABAergic, adrenergic, and peptidergic.
source: The different activation dynamics may lead to the release of different neurotransmitter and neuromodulator cocktails cPRCs are cholinergic, GABAergic, adrenergic, and peptidergic (Jokura et al., 2023; Randel et al., 2014; Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2017) and different activation patterns in the postsynaptic cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jokura et al., 2023; Randel et al., 2014; Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007; Williams et al., 2017.

claim: Similar integration of multiple stimuli can occur in Drosophila larvae, where UV/blue light and noxious mechanical stimuli are detected by the same sensory neuron.
source: Similar integration can occur in Drosophila larvae, where UV/blue light and noxious mechanical stimuli are detected by the same sensory neuron that together with other cells converges onto a circuit processing multisensory stimuli (Imambocus et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Imambocus et al., 2022.

claim: The mechanism of pressure sensation may involve the differential compression of microtubules along each ciliary branch.
source: The mechanism may involve the differential compression of microtubules along each ciliary branch (Li et al., 2022; Nasrin et al., 2021), or differential displacement of fluid inside the cilium (Bell, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Li et al., 2022; Nasrin et al., 2021.

claim: The mechanism of pressure sensation may involve differential displacement of fluid inside the cilium.
source: The mechanism may involve the differential compression of microtubules along each ciliary branch (Li et al., 2022; Nasrin et al., 2021), or differential displacement of fluid inside the cilium (Bell, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to Bell, 2008.

claim: The cPRCs have a unique multiciliated structure and are embedded in a protected environment different from fluid-exposed cilia such as hydrodynamic mechanosensory cilia.
source: The cPRCs have a unique multiciliated structure and are embedded in a protected environment different from fluid-exposed cilia such as hydrodynamic mechanosensory cilia (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by a citation to Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018.

claim: These features are hard to reconcile with current models of ciliary mechanosensation.
source: These features are hard to reconcile with current models of ciliary mechanosensation (e.g. see review by R Ferreira et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge supported by a citation to R Ferreira et al., 2019.

claim: The mechanism of pressure sensation at work in cPRCs may share more similarities with non-neuronal cells detecting pressure, such as chondrocytes and trabecular meshwork cells.
source: Instead, the mechanism of pressure sensation at work in cPRCs may share more similarities with non-neuronal cells detecting pressure, such as chondrocytes (Pattappa et al., 2019) and trabecular meshwork cells (Luo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Pattappa et al., 2019 and Luo et al., 2014.

claim: Components of the phototransduction cascade may be involved in pressure sensation.
source: Components of the phototransduction cascade may be involved in pressure sensation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings.

source: Our results indicate that the ciliary opsin required for detecting UV light is not essential for pressure sensation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

source: The mechanism by which cPRCs detect pressure in Platynereis may also characterize the few other cases of pressure sensors based on ciliated sensory cells (the crab statocyst, and the dog hair cells) (Fraser and Macdonald, 1994; Fraser and Shelmerdine, 2002).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Fraser and Macdonald, 1994; Fraser and Shelmerdine, 2002.

source: Multiciliated pressure receptors may be widespread in zooplankton, as cells with a morphology similar to the cPRCs have been observed in species across the animal phylogeny (Hernandez-Nicaise, 1984.; Baatrup, 1982; Eakin and Kuda, 1970), reviewed in Bezares-Calderón et al., 2020.

source: To our knowledge, this study provides the first functional evidence for the role of multiciliated sensory cells in pressure sensation.
evidence: This is stated as a claim about the novelty of the findings.
